headline: Homeopathic practitioner hacked to death in Natore chamber
summary: Md Anwarul Islam, 60, was attacked by unidentified criminals while working in his clinic at Chandpur Market on Wednesday night.
details: Md Anwarul Islam, a 60-year-old homeopathic practitioner, was killed in his chamber at Chandpur Market in Natore Sadar upazila on Wednesday night.
The attack occurred around 7:30 pm while the victim was working. According to police, criminals hacked him to death, though the motive behind the killing remains unclear.
Anwarul, originally from Puthia upazila in Rajshahi, had been practicing in the area for over three decades. Locals stated they were unaware of any enmity that could lead to the murder.
Police recovered the body and sent it to Natore Sadar Hospital for an autopsy. Officers are currently investigating the incident to identify and apprehend the culprits.
caption:
A 60-year-old homeopathic doctor was hacked to death in his own clinic in Natore.

Md Anwarul Islam, a 60-year-old homeopathic practitioner, was killed in his chamber at Chandpur Market in Natore Sadar upazila on Wednesday night.

The attack occurred around 7:30 pm while the victim was working. According to police, criminals hacked him to death, though the motive behind the killing remains unclear.

Anwarul, originally from Puthia upazila in Rajshahi, had been practicing in the area for over three decades. Locals stated they were unaware of any enmity that could lead to the murder.

Police recovered the body and sent it to Natore Sadar Hospital for an autopsy. Officers are currently investigating the incident to identify and apprehend the culprits.

headline: Tk 6 lakh crore: Bad loans in banking sector surpass Tk 6 lakh crore again
summary: Despite policy support and rescheduling efforts, defaulted loans now make up 32.78% of total disbursed loans, according to Bangladesh Bank.
details: Bad loans in the banking sector have once again crossed the Tk 6 lakh crore mark. As of June, defaulted loans stood at Tk 6,06,555 crore, representing 32.78% of all disbursed loans, according to Bangladesh Bank data.

In the three months leading up to June, defaulted loans increased by Tk 17,851 crore. This follows a sharp jump in bad loans after the fall of the previous government in August 2024, driven by heavy defaults from affiliated businesses like S Alam Group and Beximco.

The interim and BNP-led governments have introduced several measures to curb this, including easier loan rescheduling and a one-time exit policy. However, these initiatives have failed to significantly reduce the totals as many borrowers cannot afford the required down payments.

Bangladesh Bank spokesperson Arief Hossain Khan noted that interest continues to accumulate and is added to the defaulted sums. Some borrowers are also seeking more time, leaving many rescheduling cases pending.

Due to the fragile state of the sector, the government recently merged five crisis-hit banks—including Social Islami Bank and Union Bank—into a state-run Shariah-based bank. Most of these banks were previously dominated by the S Alam Group.

Experts warn that repeated regulatory forbearance and concessions have sent the wrong signal to the market. Former World Bank economist Zahid Hussain suggests that further relaxation could worsen the situation and that authorities must signal an end to repeated concessions.
caption:
Tk 6,06,555 crore. That is the staggering amount of bad loans currently clogging Bangladesh's banking sector.

Bad loans in the banking sector have once again crossed the Tk 6 lakh crore mark. As of June, defaulted loans stood at Tk 6,06,555 crore, representing 32.78% of all disbursed loans, according to Bangladesh Bank data.

In the three months leading up to June, defaulted loans increased by Tk 17,851 crore. This follows a sharp jump in bad loans after the fall of the previous government in August 2024, driven by heavy defaults from affiliated businesses like S Alam Group and Beximco.

The interim and BNP-led governments have introduced several measures to curb this, including easier loan rescheduling and a one-time exit policy. However, these initiatives have failed to significantly reduce the totals as many borrowers cannot afford the required down payments.

Bangladesh Bank spokesperson Arief Hossain Khan noted that interest continues to accumulate and is added to the defaulted sums. Some borrowers are also seeking more time, leaving many rescheduling cases pending.

Due to the fragile state of the sector, the government recently merged five crisis-hit banks—including Social Islami Bank and Union Bank—into a state-run Shariah-based bank. Most of these banks were previously dominated by the S Alam Group.

Experts warn that repeated regulatory forbearance and concessions have sent the wrong signal to the market. Former World Bank economist Zahid Hussain suggests that further relaxation could worsen the situation and that authorities must signal an end to repeated concessions.
